children.text: A plaza and church laid out on the Spanish colonial town plan, plus about 28 early 20th-century ancestral houses, all within one district — this is Laguna's National Historical Landmark. The first church in the Philippines dedicated to St. Anthony, a small museum and slow strolls through the lanes fill a half-day trip from Manila.
Pila is a small town on the plain between Laguna de Bay and the foothills, in the southeast of Laguna province. It lies about
79km
from Manila, and on

the National Historical Institute (today's National Historical Commission of the Philippines, NHCP) declared the heart of the town a National Historical Landmark. The Spaniards are said to have called it "La Noble Villa de Pila" (the Noble Town of Pila), a name that points to its long reputation as a refined and well-mannered place.

What makes Pila special is that the whole layout of the town has survived. Following the Spanish colonial town plan, a broad plaza sits at the center and the church, municipal building, school and the mansions of leading families surround it, and you can still see that arrangement today. The designated area is the Santa Clara Norte district, bounded by General Luna Street to the north, M.H. del Pilar Street to the east, Mabini Street to the south and Bonifacio Street to the west, and a single walk around it takes about an hour. About 35 heritage buildings remain here, and roughly 28 of them are ancestral houses (sources differ, giving 28 to 30).
If you go expecting stone mansions of the Spanish era like those in Vigan or Taal, it is a little different. Most of Pila's houses were built in the American colonial period, between the

, with stone and cement on the ground floor, a wooden upper floor, capiz-shell windows and Art Deco touches. What the town has instead is a deeper layer of time. Franciscan missionaries began their work here in
, and the
excavation at Pinagbayanan turned up pottery and Chinese ceramics from around the 10th century, showing that Pila was already a trading center before the Spaniards arrived.
The church was the first parish in the Philippines dedicated to St. Anthony (San Antonio de Padua), and it was raised to a National Shrine on
April 23, 2019

. The town is also proud of being recognized as a heritage site by both state and church. It suits travelers who enjoy history, architecture, photography and unhurried small-town walks, and it can be done as a
half-day to full-day

trip from Manila, so it combines well with Pagsanjan Falls or Nagcarlan in Laguna. It is not a polished tourist attraction but a town where people really live, and its quiet, modest atmosphere is the charm.

The three-level facade of volcanic tuff has Doric columns, and a red-brick octagonal belfry on the left makes a striking contrast. The church originally stood at Pagalangan, and was moved to its present site to escape flooding and completed in
. This facade is where the best photos are taken.

blocks.title: Old bells of the church garden

children.text: A few old bells are on display in the garden in front of the church. The oldest was cast in
; it is said to have been hidden during the British occupation of Manila and is considered the third-oldest church bell in the Philippines.
The broad lawn, lined with tall trees along its edges, is the town's living room. On one side stands the municipal building put up in
, and there is also a historical marker announcing the National Historical Landmark designation. The marker records that Felizardo de Rivera laid out the framework of the town.

The mansions of old families such as the Alava, Agra, Rivera and Relova stand along Bonifacio Street and Rivera Street and the area around them. Wide capiz windows, wrought-iron railings and side staircases are common features, and some houses use the ground floor as a cafe or shop, so it is pleasant to stroll and look.
This small museum occupies the former Escuela Pia building on Burzagom Street. It shows pre-Hispanic finds from the
excavation, such as pottery, plates, jars and Chinese ceramics. Admission is said to be by donation, so it is an easy stop.

A two-story stone building beside the church, with a long arched arcade. It was once used as the convent attached to the church. You can frame the courtyard, the church facade and the plaza in a single shot, so it counts as a photo spot.

With its gilded altar, long nave (the central aisle) and statue of St. Anthony, the interior is a living church where Mass is still held. It is known to keep part of the saint's relics, and pilgrims keep coming.

blocks.title: Pailah Festival and the Feast of St. Anthony

children.text: The Pailah Festival, held around
April
each year, is a harvest thanksgiving whose name is formed from the initials of rice (Palay), fish (Isda), antique carvings (Lilok antigo) and plants (Halaman). On the Feast of St. Anthony on
June 13
, the area around the church fills with banners and processions.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: A day trip from Manila: plaza, church and old houses on foot

children.text: Leave Manila (by car via SLEX toward Calamba, or by bus bound for Santa Cruz)
Arrive in Pila; look around the plaza, the municipal building and the historical marker
San Antonio de Padua Church — the facade and belfry, the old bells in the garden, the altar inside
Walk past Liceo de Pila to the ancestral houses on Bonifacio and Rivera streets
Lunch at a restaurant near the plaza or at a cafe in a restored old house
Visit the Pila Museum (if you are there on a weekday)
Head back to Manila, arriving in the early evening
The museum is said to open mainly on weekdays, so it may be closed if you visit on a weekend. On weekends, plan around the plaza, the church and the outsides of the old houses.

items.title: Full-day route
items.subtitle: Pila combined with Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery

children.text: Leave Manila
Look around the Pila plaza and church
Stroll the street of ancestral houses and visit the museum (weekdays)
Lunch, and a taste of Pila's local snacks
Drive to Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery (closed Mondays, closes around 4 PM)
Head back to Manila via Santa Cruz and Calamba

Both sites close fairly early, so it is safest to finish Pila in the morning and reach Nagcarlan early in the afternoon. By public transport you have to go through Santa Cruz, which makes the day very tight.
Take a bus bound for Santa Cruz (Laguna) from PITX, Buendia, Cubao or Alabang in Manila. Companies such as DLTB, JAC Liner, LLI and HM Transport operate it, taking about
3 to 3 hours 30 minutes
at a fare of about
Tell the conductor in advance that you are getting off in 「Pila town proper (Poblacion)」. The route passes Calamba and Los Baños and reaches Pila via Victoria.
If you have gone all the way to Santa Cruz, you can transfer near the market to a jeepney bound for Pila. It takes about
15–30 minutes
and costs about
. Jeepneys run from early morning until around
7 PM
Timetables and fares change often. Check the last bus back, and plan to leave the plaza before
5 PM
to be safe.
Take SLEX and leave at the Calamba exit, then follow the national road through Los Baños, Bay and Victoria into Pila. It is about
79km
from Manila and takes
2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours 30 minutes
depending on traffic. Turn left off the national road and you will come to the plaza. The streets are narrow, so leave the car near the plaza and church and explore on foot.
If you are traveling in a group, it is convenient to hire a van with a driver for the day. For Pila, Nagcarlan and Pagsanjan together, it is common to bargain to about
per day. A Grab booking from Manila to Pila may not be accepted or may cost far more, so a pre-booked vehicle is the sure option.
The plaza, church, museum and ancestral houses are all in one area, so walking is enough. To reach spots along the national road or farther neighborhoods, a tricycle takes about
5–10 minutes
and costs about
(negotiable).
The dry season,
November–May
, is the best time to walk around Pila. Since this is a trip on foot among old houses, dry weather and clear skies also make for better photos. From
December to February
mornings and evenings are cool, but from
March to May
midday temperatures climb to
and the middle of the plaza offers little escape from the sun, so it is best to look around in the early morning or late afternoon.
During the
June–October

rainy season, afternoon showers are frequent, and when a typhoon passes the area around Laguna de Bay can flood. Remembering that the church moved to its present site because of flooding, you can feel the town's long relationship with water. If you go in the rainy season, bring an umbrella and dry shoes and check the typhoon forecast.
Event dates are worth planning around. The Pailah Festival around
April
, the Feast of St. Anthony on
June 13
and Holy Week (
late March–April

) bring crowds to the church and a livelier atmosphere than usual. If you would rather see the architecture quietly, choose a weekday. Festival dates change from year to year, so check the latest announcements.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
There are few hotels in Pila itself, but small resorts and homestays with pools are scattered toward the rice fields and the lakeshore. Rates are about
per night. To widen your choices, you can stay in Santa Cruz, Pagsanjan or Los Baños,
20–40 minutes
away by car. Most travelers make it a day trip from Manila.

Around the plaza there are a few Filipino home-cooking restaurants and cafes in restored old houses where you can have simple meals such as sinigang, crispy pata and grilled seafood. Pila is also a place where snacks made from coconut and rice have developed. Puto cut into squares, bibingka with macapuno (soft, jelly-like coconut meat), buko pie and espasol suit Laguna's snack tradition well. As a Pila specialty, hinalo, a black-glutinous-rice kalamay-type sweet made during the Christmas season, is known, and the church is said to sell biscotti cookies stamped with the face of St. Anthony.
Start by standing in the middle of the plaza and looking around. The church, municipal building, Liceo and museum are all in view, and you can see at a glance how the town was laid out.

The church is still a place where Mass is held. Wear clothes that cover your shoulders and knees, and refrain from taking photos or walking around during Mass. Sunday Masses are said to be held several times between
and
, so check the parish office's announcements.

Most ancestral houses are private homes where people live. Photograph the exteriors and what you can see from the street, and if you want to see inside, ask first at a guide desk such as the Pila Historical Society.
The facade is best photographed in the light of
. The color contrast between the red brick of the belfry and the gray tuff walls comes out most vividly then.
The museum and some of the houses do not keep regular hours. Go on a weekday morning and, if you need to be sure, inquire beforehand.
Many restaurants, shops and tricycles take cash only. Bring plenty of small change.
When planning, it is efficient to combine Pila with other inland Laguna towns in the same direction, such as Pagsanjan Falls, Nagcarlan and Liliw.
Opening hours, event schedules and church Mass times are most accurate from local announcements. Check once more the day before you leave.

The ancestral houses of Pila are not tourist facilities but people's homes. Do not enter through the gates or photograph through the windows. Avoid taking pictures of people's faces without permission as well.
There are reports of the museum actually being closed. To avoid traveling all that way and missing it, visit on a weekday and confirm beforehand if needed.
In the middle of the plaza there is little shade during the day, and there is a risk of heatstroke in summer. Bring a hat, water and sunscreen.
The main road (national road) carries many large buses and trucks. Do not step into the road when crossing or when taking photos.
In the rainy season, typhoons and lake overflow can block roads. Check the weather forecast and road conditions before you leave.
Keep your valuables on your person, and do not walk alone through dimly lit back streets after dark.
